This week, I was proud to announce $65 million in funding to replace our state’s aging rural infrastructure through the Competitive Highway Bridge Program (CHBP) – a grant program I helped create in 2018 to fund highway bridge replacement and rehabilitation projects on roads that serve rural communities. Maine will receive 16 percent of the $408 million awarded nationally through the CHBP this cycle.

The funding will support 15 projects across our state, including 11 bridge replacements across seven counties and four bridge deck replacements on I-95 in Penobscot County. Many of these bridges are more than 50 years old and have exceeded their original design life, creating safety risks for the drivers who rely on them every day. Replacing them is a critical effort that will make travel safer, create jobs, and better connect rural communities across Maine to the rest of our state and nation.

Projects include:

Caratunk (Main St.) – built in 1922, crossing Pleasant Pond Stream

Caratunk (Pleasant Pond Rd.) – built in 1945, crossing Pleasant Pond Stream

Carmel (Fuller Rd.) – built in 1963, crossing Harvey Brook

Chesterville (Mace Rd.) – built in 1950, crossing McGurdy Stream

Cornville (Huff Rd.) – built in 1936, crossing Wesserunsett Stream

Embden (Kennebec River Rd.) – built in 1934, crossing Martin Stream

Lisbon/Bowdoin line (Burrough Rd.) – built in 1936, crossing the Little River

Orland (Bald Mountain Rd.) – built in 1951, crossing Moosehorn Creek

Salem Township (Howard Rd.) – built in 1974, crossing the West Branch Carrabasset River

Sangerville (Silvers Mills Rd.) – built in 1954, crossing French Mills Brook

Topsham (Cathance Rd.) – built in 1920, crossing the Cathance River

Howland (I-95 NB and SB) – bridge decks to be replaced over the Piscataquis River

Old Town (I-95 NB and SB) – bridge decks to be replaced over Pushaw Stream

The President’s Budget Request is just that, a request. To compensate for years of underfunding, the Administration proposes to increase defense funding significantly and recognizes the annual appropriations process as the best way to provide additional funds. The request for just one DDG-51, the workhorse of the U.S. Navy, is insufficient to counter the ever-growing Chinese fleet, which now exceeds the size of the American Navy, as well as other global threats.  
 
While there are some improvements over last year’s domestic discretionary budget request, including full support for the Pell Grant program, the request has several shortcomings. For example, the proposal includes unwarranted funding cuts in biomedical research.  It would also terminate worthwhile programs like LIHEAP, which helps low-income families and seniors to pay their energy bills during the cold winter and hot summer months, and TRIO, which assists low-income, first-generation students in pursuing higher education.  Job Corps, which helps students from troubled backgrounds gain the skills and education they need to enter the workforce, join the military, or pursue higher education, would also be phased out.  These are proven programs that I strongly support.
 
Another program that is important to rural America’s economy is the Essential Air Service program.  The Administration is proposing deep cuts in the EAS program.    
 
After careful review, Congress decisively rejected these particular cuts last year.
 
While the Administration proposes a budget, Congress holds the power of the purse. The Senate Appropriations Committee will now hold hearings with cabinet members and agency heads to review these recommendations and to explore other fiscally responsible proposals.  I hope my colleagues on the other side of the aisle, who too often worked over the last year to impede the appropriations process and shut down federal agencies, will abandon their harmful tactics and work with us to govern responsibly.

B000490.text:
I was honored to emcee and deliver an update from Congress at yesterday’s Ham & Eggs Legislative Breakfast at Fort Valley State University. Every year it brings together local, state, federal, and agricultural leaders along with educators and students.

Tariffs, wars, and disaster relief along with federal cuts to basic needs, like healthcare, housing, education, and energy programs are making it more expensive to live and work in agriculture and rural America. But Democrats and Republicans were in the room to talk through these challenges and find ways we can work together – in government, industry, and academia – to meet these challenges and help Georgia continue to grow!

This week, I was in Quitman, Clay, Early, Calhoun, Randolph, Marion, Schley, Macon, Taylor, Thomas, Grady, Decatur, and Mitchell Counties. I met with agricultural producers, local Farm Bureaus, the Georgia Peanut, Pecan, Cotton, and Forestry Commissions as well as Georgia Green Industry, Georgia Fruit and Vegetable Growers Association, and the Randolph County Hospital Administration.

I heard from them about how tariffs, high agricultural input costs, and military conflicts are affecting the cost of doing business and the cost of living. I was able to share the work I am doing in Congress to protect programs and funding that support our hardworking ag producers weather these uncertain times. When I first ran for State Representative back in 1992, my aspiration was to represent my hometown of Tarkio, Missouri. I was a twenty-seven year old farmer who just wanted to stand up for a way of life and his community.  I never could have imagined where that decision would take me.   

For 8 years in the Missouri House and Senate, I fought for Northwest Missourians. From deregulating vehicle inspections, to standing for chain gangs, to securing funding for rural schools in the desegregation fight, I never lost sight of why I was sent to Jefferson City. Then, in 2000, the good, hardworking people of Missouri’s Sixth District entrusted me to be their voice in Congress.    

For 26 years, I have had the privilege of serving, culminating in becoming the Chairman of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and passing some of the most significant legislation in our nation’s history.  The responsibility entrusted to me is not something I have ever taken for granted. Not for a single day.   

What I’m most proud of is the work my team did when Washington made life harder for the people of Missouri’s Sixth. Together, we stood with hundreds of thousands of Missourians in their toughest moments.  We helped them cut through red tape and navigate a system that often felt stacked against them.  We got them answers and fought to deliver real results when they needed them most.   

I’ve said all of that to say this: After considerable reflection, 2026 will be my final year in Congress.  This wasn’t an easy decision, but it’s the right one. I believe in making room for the next generation. It’s time to pass the torch and allow a new guard of conservative leaders to step forward and chart a path forward for Missourians.    

That doesn’t mean I’m slowing down, not even close.  As I enter the 4th quarter of my life, I have more left in me. As many of you know, I don't let grass grow under my feet. We’ve still got a lot of work to do. I’m going to fight to protect Missouri interests as we work to shape this year’s Highway Bill. I plan to finish this last term the same way I started, full speed ahead.   

Maintaining our strong democratic republic will always depend on good people stepping up to serve from every corner of our great nation. I’m grateful for my colleagues in both parties, for the people I’ve worked alongside, and even for the opponents who challenged me and made me better. Public service isn’t easy. It takes hard work, humility, a thick skin, and a willingness to fight for what’s right.   

At the end of the day, I’m still the farmer from Northwest Missouri. You’ll find me back home on the farm nearly every weekend, after all, it is planting season. In fact, I’ll probably be on a tractor this weekend. And come Monday, I’ll be heading back through Kansas City on my way to D.C. to keep doing the job you sent me there to do.   From the bottom of my heart, thank you.    

It has been the honor of a lifetime.

In 1961, Congress enacted the Sports Broadcasting Act, granting limited antitrust immunity to allow professional football teams to collectively license the “sponsored telecasts” of their games to national broadcast networks. 

Courts have recognized that “sponsored telecasting” refers to broadcasts financed through advertising and made available free to the public. Shaw v. Dallas Cowboys Football Club, Ltd., 172 F.3d 299, 301 (3d Cir. 1999).

The modern distribution environment differs substantially from the conditions that precipitated this exemption. 

Instead of a small number of free broadcast networks, the NFL now licenses games simultaneously to subscription streaming platforms, premium cable networks, and technology companies operating under different business models. 

To the extent collectively licensed game packages are placed behind subscription paywalls, these arrangements may no longer align with the statutory concept of sponsored telecasting or the consumer-access rationale underlying the antitrust exemption.

That’s why, as chair of the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Competition Policy, and Consumer Rights, I urged the DOJ to examine the Sports Broadcasting Act and its applicability to current media landscape. 

I’m glad they’re tackling this.

The report also presents new information about China’s use of shadow fleet tankers, at times manned by military and intelligence personnel, to acquire tens of millions of barrels of crude oil at a deep discount to market prices.

"For purposes of this report, the “shadow fleet” serves as the umbrella term for all vessels engaged in deceptive operations to circumvent sanctions or oversight.  As of March 2026, @Kpler, a commodity data and analytics firm that tracks global vessel movements, cargo flows, and trade patterns using satellite imagery, AIS signals, and machine learning, tracks 2,291 such tankers comprising roughly 16.8 percent of active commercial wet cargo vessels above 5,000 gross tonnage. Approximately 45 percent are formally sanctioned."

The bottom line: sanctions do not isolate adversaries but instead they consolidate an oil system centered on China.

As part of our weekly series, my office is highlighting how our constituent services team makes a difference in the lives of the people of the Eighth Congressional District.

Last year, Michael was hospitalized and diagnosed with congenital spinal stenosis and four herniated discs. He receives medical coverage through CHAMPVA. To maintain eligibility in the program, Michael needed to show that he was a full-time student. His school provided the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs with the required documentation, but the VA took months to process it, causing his medical bills to pile up and leaving him unable to receive necessary medical care.

For months, he contacted the VA and was told his case was marked as urgent, but nothing changed.

He turned to my office for help. My staff contacted the VA to confirm the agency was working to verify his eligibility. Through my team’s communications with the VA, we were able to resolve the problem.

“Within a week, my insurance was finally verified, and I was able to begin physical therapy. After all the calls and escalations we made to the VA, I was stunned – and incredibly grateful – that Raja’s office was able to resolve this so quickly.

Thank you, Raja, for helping me finally begin my recovery.”

If you need help with a federal agency, please contact my office at 847-413-1959 or IL08.HelpLine@mail.house.gov.

Kira built the project around a challenge many young athletes know well: balancing academics, athletics, personal pressures, sportsmanship, and leadership responsibilities. Her response was thoughtful and practical, creating space for student-athletes to build confidence, manage stress, strengthen peer support, and lead with empathy and accountability.

As Co-Chair of the Bipartisan Mental Health and Substance Use Disorder Task Force, I know young people like Kira have a great deal to teach us. Her perspective reflects the pressures many students are navigating, and her initiative reflects the kind of leadership we should be encouraging and elevating.

Kira is a remarkable young leader already making a difference, and I look forward to carrying insights like hers into the broader work of strengthening mental health support for students in our schools and communities.

I was honored to attend a special ceremony this morning at the Wyoming County Courthouse alongside Senator Lisa Baker and Representative Tina Pickett recognizing individuals who have voted for 50 consecutive years.

Voting is one of our most important civic responsibilities, and this level of consistency and commitment speaks volumes about the strength of our community and the value of having your voice heard. It’s also why efforts like the SAVE (Safeguard American Voter Eligibility) Act are so important to ensuring the integrity of our elections and protecting the ability of individuals, like the nine honored today, to continue exercising their right to vote.

Thank you to those recognized for setting such a powerful example of dedication, responsibility, and engagement in our democratic process.

Great to join the Wyoming County Chamber of Commerce this morning at their annual Legislative Breakfast in Tunkhannock. I appreciated the opportunity to participate in a panel discussion alongside local and state leaders to discuss the issues that matter most to Wyoming County, including the work we’re doing to support small businesses. Through my work on the House Committee on Small Business, we’re focused on lowering taxes, providing regulatory relief, and expanding access to capital. It is great to see firsthand the individuals and businesses impacted by these policies.

Thank you to Chamber President Francene Pisano for hosting a great event and for her continued leadership in strengthening partnerships and expanding opportunities for local businesses. Also in attendance were Senator Lisa Baker, State Representative Tina Pickett, Wyoming County Commissioners Ernie King, Rick Wilbur, and Tom Henry, District Attorney Joe Peters, along with Tunkhannock Mayor Stacey Huber, all doing important work on behalf of Wyoming County.

These are important conversations, and I’m grateful for the opportunity to hear directly from local leaders and continue working together to move our communities forward.

Today I joined the Williamsport/Lycoming Chamber of Commerce for their Pennsylvania’s Power Future event to discuss the forces driving today’s energy challenges, the growing demands of the data center economy, and what business leaders should consider as they navigate this pivotal moment. We discussed Pennsylvania’s growing energy demand and the need to strengthen the grid, noting that while the Commonwealth is a net electricity exporter, burdensome permitting, a lack of new generation since 2019, and insufficient investment in generation and transmission are limiting in-state growth and long-term stability needed to attract businesses and develop the workforce. Thank you to Chamber President & CEO Jason Fink for moderating a strong panel including Christine Martin, President of PPL Electric Utilities, Becky Ford of AWS, and Representative David Rowe. Always good to see Representative Joe Hamm and Representative Jamie Flick who joined us for this important conversation.

Afterward, we visited the Williamsport Lumber Yards Sports Complex with the Chamber and Christine Martin to see firsthand the continued investment and growth happening in the region. Set to open very soon, this 28-acre complex will feature six lighted turf fields, a collegiate-size field, and modern amenities for tournaments, leagues, and community events. The project is expected to attract nearly 175,000 visitors annually and serve as a strong economic driver for the region.

I was glad to join Representative Leadbetter’s Farmers Breakfast this morning in Columbia County. It was a strong turnout, with many farmers in attendance and a great opportunity to connect directly with the hardworking men and women who keep Pennsylvania agriculture moving.

Eastern North Carolina, here’s an inspiring story that highlights the bright future awaiting our young people right here at home.

During the State of the Union Address, I had the honor of hosting a native son of Hyde County, Nathanael Simmons, a remarkable 17-year-old, eighth-generation farmer who exemplifies the spirit of resilience and hope in our part of the state. While many farmers face challenges, Nathanael stands as a shining example for the next generation, reminding us that our roots can lead us to incredible heights.

His presence at the State of the Union coincided with an extraordinary moment in space exploration. NASA's Artemis II mission is truly revolutionary, aiming to "unlock the next generation of space exploration." Just 42 days after the State of the Union, this brave crew traveled further from Earth than any humans have before, reaching an astonishing 252,756 miles—surpassing the Apollo 13 record set in 1970.

The mission serves not just as a testament to human ingenuity but as a challenge to all of us: let’s ensure that records like this inspire rather than intimidate. It's time for our young people, especially those from eastern NC, to dream big and pursue their passions, whether in agriculture or aviation sciences after completing first-rate programs like those at Elizabeth City State University, or in any field or school they choose.

While at the State of the Union, we discussed with the astronauts the food that they would eat in space. It was heartwarming to hear Christina Hammock Koch, who grew up in Jacksonville, is a graduate of the North Carolina School of Science and Mathematics, and an NC State University alum, talk about her love for space cuisine. If she can reach for the stars from eastern North Carolina, imagine what our young people can achieve.

Let Nathanael's and this fantastic crew’s journey be a reminder that while many leave to seek opportunities elsewhere, there is tremendous potential here in eastern North Carolina to create a bright future. Your dreams matter. Your roots are your strength. Embrace them, and let them propel you to new heights.

Together, let's inspire the next generation to stay or return as innovators and leaders who will cultivate our land and explore the stars, reclaiming the future of eastern North Carolina. Artemis II, eastern NC welcomes you back home!

Stephen Woofter of Gaston has dedicated his life to service, with 25 years as a math teacher and 27 in the military across active duty in the National Guard and Reserve in both the Army and Air Force. A true hero, he served as a parachute rigger, infantryman, and intelligence specialist in Iraq, Afghanistan, and Qatar.

For Stephen, the call to serve continues beyond the uniform through VFW Post 3702, AMVETS Post 320, and American Legion Post 38. He supports veterans by helping them access care—transportation, resources, and IT support. Beyond his work with veterans, Stephen contributes to his community by maintaining trails with the Potomac Appalachian Trail Club and helping wherever needed.

His lifelong service and responsibility are evident, and we proudly honor Stephen Woofter for his dedication to veterans and community service, leaving a lasting impact on Northampton County and across the East.

MCAS Cherry Point is the world’s largest Marine Corps air station with the only 24/7, year-round airfield operation. It plays a vital role in our national defense and contributes over $2.6 billion to eastern North Carolina’s economy.

I'm glad cooler heads prevailed and a ceasefire is in place, but before anyone starts treating Iran like a good faith negotiating partner, let me be precise about who we are dealing with.

This is a regime that massacred over 30,000 of its own citizens in January, when ordinary people took to the streets demanding a better life. They cut the internet so the world could not watch. They buried bodies in mass graves under cover of night, charged grieving families for the bullets used to kill their children, and dispatched security forces into hospitals to finish off the wounded. Then, with extraordinary cynicism, they called the dead terrorists, blamed foreign agents, and falsified every body count. A government willing to do that to its own people will do anything to its enemies.

When President Trump set his deadline to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the regime's response was entirely consistent with its character. They herded women and children to power plants and bridges, ordering them to form human chains around critical infrastructure. They lowered the minimum age for war roles to twelve years old. An IRGC commander appeared on state television and told parents, openly and without shame, to send their children to the checkpoints. This is the same regime that marched young boys into minefields during the Iran-Iraq War to clear the path for tanks. The calculus has never changed.

On the infrastructure question, President Trump was right. Those bridges and power plants are not civilian assets in any meaningful sense. Every kilowatt of electricity and every road in that country serves a regime that has killed over a thousand Americans, funded Hezbollah, armed the Houthis, and systematically exported chaos to every corner of the region for 47 years. Targeting the machinery of terrorism is not a war crime, and allowing it to operate unchallenged is not diplomacy.

My position has never changed: no American boots on the ground. I've personally fought in a war that dragged on for years without clear objectives or a defined end state, and I've seen what happens when conflict becomes open-ended, when every day means more American blood spilled on foreign soil with no path to victory. War demands absolute clarity of purpose, and anything less prolongs the cost in American lives. We cannot ignore the broader battlefield either. For years, China has financed and emboldened adversaries who exist to undermine American standing in the world, and every conflict we enter without winning is an invitation for Beijing to fill the void. President Trump understands that. Forcing NATO allies to carry their share of the burden is exactly what leadership looks like.

A ceasefire has real value, and no one who has seen war up close is eager for more of it, but a durable agreement demands more than a handshake over a temporary pause. History has shown us that we cannot afford to give Iran the benefit of the doubt. Any final deal must include zero nuclear weapons, zero enriched uranium stockpiles, unimpeded passage through the Strait of Hormuz, and the verifiable dismantling of Iran's terror export network. Those are not opening positions, they are the minimum conditions for taking this regime seriously at the table.

We negotiate from a position of strength, or we do not negotiate at all.

Thankfully there’s no shortage of sport on TV this month!

WORLD_GERMANY_CHANCELLOR.text: Es gibt ein Chance auf Frieden im Nahen Osten. Deutschland hat daran ein fundamentales Interesse: Die Stabilität der Region sowie die Entwicklung der Weltwirtschaft und unserer eigenen hängen davon ab. Wir sind bereit, Verantwortung zu übernehmen und Frieden zu sichern.
Für die Bürgerinnen und Bürger Deutschlands.

I welcome the two-week ceasefire agreed by the United States and Iran last night. 

We thank Pakistan for its mediation. 

The aim now is to negotiate a lasting end to the war. We are in close coordination with our partners on this matter.

Ich begrüße die zweiwöchige Waffenruhe, auf die sich USA und Iran in der Nacht verständigt haben. 

Unser Dank gilt Pakistan für die Vermittlung.

Ziel muss es jetzt sein, ein dauerhaftes Kriegsende auszuhandeln. Wir stehen dazu in engem Austausch mit unseren Partnern.

Wir trauern um Christian Schwarz-Schilling. Er war ein verdienter Bundesminister und überzeugter Europäer. Als Hoher Repräsentant für Bosnien und Herzegowina hat er sich mit ganzer Kraft für Frieden und Versöhnung auf dem Balkan eingesetzt. Sein Einsatz bleibt uns Verpflichtung.

WORLD_INDIA_PM.text:
महान समाज सुधारक महात्मा फुले की 200वीं जयंती वर्ष के समारोहों का शुभारंभ हो रहा है। उन्होंने अपना पूरा जीवन शिक्षा, ज्ञान और जन कल्याण को समर्पित कर दिया। वे कैसे आज भी करोड़ों देशवासियों के लिए प्रेरणापुंज बने हुए हैं, इसी को लेकर मैंने इस आलेख में अपने विचार रखे हैं।

https://nm-4.com/UFQgrq

आपण महात्मा फुले यांच्या जयंतीच्या द्विशताब्दी वर्षात पाऊल ठेवत असल्याच्या पार्श्वभूमीवर, ते कशा प्रकारे अनेक लोकांसाठी मार्गदर्शक दीपस्तंभ ठरले आहेत तसेच त्यांनी शिक्षण, अध्ययन आणि सर्वांच्या कल्याणावर दिलेला भर आजच्या युगातही कसा समर्पक आहे, याबद्दलचे काही विचार लेखणीतून उतरवले आहेत.

https://nm-4.com/iPWs1u

As we begin the 200th birth anniversary celebrations of Mahatma Phule, penned a few thoughts on how he is a guiding light for several people and how his emphasis on education, learning and welfare of all are relevant in today’s age.

https://nm-4.com/3bqfP8

महात्मा ज्योतिराव फुले यांच्या जयंतीदिनी, समता, न्याय आणि शिक्षण या मूल्यांसाठी आपले जीवन समर्पित करणाऱ्या या द्रष्ट्या समाजसुधारकाला अभिवादन करतो. महिला आणि उपेक्षितांच्या हक्कांचा लढा सुरु करणारेही तेच होते. त्यांच्या प्रयत्नांमुळे शिक्षण हे सक्षमीकरणाचे एक शक्तिशाली साधन बनले. यावर्षी, आपण त्यांच्या जयंतीच्या द्विशताब्दी वर्षात पाऊल ठेवत आहोत. सामाजिक प्रगतीच्या वाटचालीत त्यांचे विचार सर्वांना सदैव मार्गदर्शन करत राहोत.

On the birth anniversary of Mahatma Jyotirao Phule, paying tributes to a visionary social reformer who dedicated his life to the ideals of equality, justice and education. He was also a pioneer in championing the rights of women and the marginalised. Through his efforts, education became a powerful instrument of empowerment. This year, we mark the start of his 200th birth anniversary celebrations. May his thoughts continue to guide everyone in the pursuit of societal progress.

WORLD_FRANCE_PRESIDENT.text:
Très heureux de rencontrer Sa Sainteté le Pape Léon XIV.

Nous portons une même conviction : face aux fractures du monde, l’action pour la paix est un devoir et une exigence. La France œuvrera toujours pour le dialogue, la justice et la fraternité entre les peuples.

I have just spoken with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam.
            
I expressed France’s full solidarity in the face of the indiscriminate strikes carried out by Israel in Lebanon today, which resulted in a very high number of civilian casualties. We condemn these strikes in the strongest possible terms.

They pose a direct threat to the sustainability of the ceasefire that has just been reached. Lebanon must be fully covered by it.

I reiterated the need to preserve Lebanon’s territorial integrity and France’s determination to support the efforts of the Lebanese authorities to uphold the country’s sovereignty and implement the Hezbollah disarmament plan.

Je viens de m’entretenir avec le Président libanais Joseph Aoun ainsi qu’avec le Premier ministre Nawaf Salam. 
 
Je leur ai exprimé la pleine solidarité de la France face aux frappes indiscriminées menées par Israël au Liban aujourd’hui, qui ont fait de très nombreuses victimes civiles. Nous les condamnons avec la plus grande fermeté. 

Ces frappes menacent directement la pérennité du cessez-le-feu qui vient d’être conclu. Le Liban doit impérativement en faire partie. 

J’ai redit la nécessité de préserver l’intégrité territoriale du Liban et la détermination de la France à soutenir les efforts des autorités libanaises en faveur de la souveraineté du pays et de la mise en œuvre du plan de désarmement du Hezbollah.

I spoke today with Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian, as well as with U.S. President Donald Trump.
                                           
I told both of them that their decision to accept a ceasefire was the best possible one.
                        
I expressed my hope that the ceasefire will be fully respected by each of the belligerents, across all areas of confrontation, including in Lebanon. This is a necessary condition for the ceasefire to be credible and lasting.

It must open the way to comprehensive negotiations capable of ensuring security for all in the Middle East.

Any agreement will have to address the concerns raised by Iran’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs, as well as its regional policy and its actions obstructing navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.

This is how a strong and lasting peace can be built, with the support of all those who are able to contribute to it. France will play its full part, in close coordination with its partners in the Middle East.

This is also what I discussed today in my exchanges with the leaders of Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Lebanon, and Iraq.

Je me suis entretenu aujourd’hui avec le Président iranien Massoud Pezeshkian, ainsi qu’avec le Président américain Donald Trump. 
                     
À tous deux, j’ai indiqué que leur décision d’accepter un cessez-le-feu était la meilleure possible. 

J’ai exprimé mon espoir que le cessez-le-feu soit pleinement respecté par chacun des belligérants, sur tous les terrains d’affrontement, y compris au Liban. C’est une condition nécessaire pour que ce cessez-le-feu soit crédible et durable.

Il doit ouvrir la voie à une négociation d’ensemble permettant d’assurer la sécurité de tous au Moyen-Orient.

Tout accord devra apporter des réponses aux inquiétudes que suscitent les programmes nucléaire et balistique de l’Iran mais aussi sa politique régionale et ses mesures d’entrave à la navigation dans le détroit d’Ormuz.

C’est ainsi qu’une paix robuste et durable pourra être bâtie, avec le concours de tous ceux qui peuvent y contribuer. La France y prendra toute sa part, en liaison étroite avec ses partenaires au Moyen-Orient.

C’est ce que j’ai également évoqué dans mes échanges ce jour avec les dirigeants du Qatar, des Émirats arabes unis, du Liban et de l’Irak.
